title: Genesis 35. The Cup of Return.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 35. The Cup of Return.
God said to Jacob: Arise, go up to Bethel, and dwell there.
Make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau.
After the silence of chapter thirty-four, God speaks.
The chapter with no divine word is followed by a chapter where God commands return.
The Cup of violence is answered by the Cup of return.
The first word after the silence is a command to go back to the place where the promise was first given.
Bethel.
The place where Jacob slept on a stone.
The place where he saw a stairway between earth and heaven.
The place where he said if.
The place where he poured oil on a pillar and named it the House of God.
God says: go back there.
Go back to where I met you when you had nothing.
The covenant's timeline is being reset.
Return to where it started.
Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him:
Put away the foreign gods that are among you.
Purify yourselves.
Change your garments.
Three commands.
Put away.
Purify.
Change.
After his silence in chapter thirty-four,
the silence that created space for his sons' violence, Jacob finally acts.
Not with a sword.
Not with a scheme.
With a command to cleanse.
The father who was silent now leads.
The foreign gods.
The household has been carrying idols.
Rachel's teraphim, stolen from Laban, hidden under a camel's saddle, lied about,
may be among them.
The spoils from Shechem,
the women and children taken as plunder after the slaughter,
may have brought their gods.
The Cup of the covenant has been carrying idols inside it since chapter thirty-one.
Now, finally, they are named.
Let us arise and go up to Bethel.
I will make there an altar to God,
who answered me in the day of my distress,
and has been with me wherever I have gone.
The conditional if of Bethel has become a testimony.
God answered me.
God has been with me.
The man who said if God will be with me now says:
He was with me.
The vow that started as a bargain has become a confession.
The vessel that set terms now acknowledges that the terms were met,
not because the vessel was worthy,
but because the One who poured was faithful.
They gave to Jacob all the foreign gods in their hands and the rings that were in their ears.
Jacob hid them under the oak that was near Shechem.
Buried.
Under the oak at Shechem.
The same place where Jacob bought land and built an altar,
El Elohe Yisrael.
The same city where his sons committed slaughter.
The covenant place becomes the burial place of idols.
The Cup that was carrying false gods is now emptied of them.
The hidden is buried.
The mixed is separated.
The vessel is being cleaned, not perfectly, not completely, but truly.
They journeyed.
And a terror of God was upon the cities that were around them.
They did not pursue the sons of Jacob.
After chapter thirty-four,
where Jacob feared the Canaanites would gather against him and destroy his house,
God puts terror on them instead.
Jacob said: I will be destroyed.
God said: No.
You will not.
The sons killed with swords.
God protects with fear.
The contrast is absolute.
Human violence produced fear.
Divine terror produced safety.
The Cup that was stained at Shechem is now shielded by the God who was silent during the stain.
Jacob came to Luz, that is, Bethel, in the land of Canaan,
he and all the people who were with him.
He built an altar there and called the place El Bethel,
God of the House of God,
because there God had revealed Himself to him when he fled from his brother.
The return.
The stone Jacob set up in chapter twenty-eight is now an altar.
The place of the dream becomes the place of worship.
The fugitive who slept alone on a rock now arrives with a household.
The man who poured oil on a pillar now builds an altar.
The place that was a dream is now a dwelling.
The if has become El.
Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died.
She was buried below Bethel under the oak.
He called its name Allon Bacuth, Oak of Weeping.
Rebekah's nurse.
The woman who served Rebekah.
Who accompanied her from Paddan-aram when she went to marry Isaac.
Who traveled with the family that carried the promise.
Rebekah herself is never mentioned again in Genesis, her death is unrecorded.
The woman who deceived Isaac, who favored Jacob,
who engineered the stolen blessing, disappears from the text.
But her nurse is honored with a named grave.
The Cup of return carries the Cup of loss.
The journey home includes a funeral.
God appeared to Jacob again when he came from Paddan-aram,
and blessed him.
God appeared again.
The dream returns as reality.
The God who was silent in chapter thirty-four,
who protected with terror on the journey, now is present.
Light intensifying: silence, protection, presence.
God said to him: Your name is Jacob.
Your name shall no longer be called Jacob,
but Israel shall be your name.
And He called his name Israel.
The name change, confirmed.
At Peniel, the wrestler changed Jacob's name to Israel.
But since then, the text has continued to call him Jacob.
Now God Himself confirms it.
The name given in the dark at the river is now spoken in the light at Bethel.
The identity that was received in wrestling is now sealed in worship.
The deceiver's old name is retired.
The wrestler's new name is given,
not by a man in the dark,
but by God in the open.
God said to him: I am El Shaddai.
Be fruitful and multiply.
A nation and a company of nations shall come from you.
Kings shall come from your body.
The land I gave to Abraham and Isaac,
to you I give it,
and to your offspring after you I give the land.
El Shaddai.
The same name used with Abraham at the covenant of circumcision.
The same name Isaac used when he blessed Jacob.
The covenant name carries the covenant promise: fruitfulness, nations, kings, land.
All the elements.
Spoken to the third generation.
Abraham received it at ninety-nine.
Isaac received it at Gerar.
Jacob receives it at Bethel, the place where he said if,
the place where he is now called Israel.
Kings shall come from your body.
The first time kings are mentioned in the covenant promise.
Not just nations.
Not just offspring like dust.
Kings.
The Cup that was held by a deceiver, cracked by a wrestler,
stained by violence, now carries the promise of thrones.
The vessel that was cleaned at Shechem and confirmed at Bethel will produce kings.
God went up from him in the place where He spoke with him.
Jacob set up a pillar of stone in the place where He spoke with him,
a pillar of stone.
He poured out a drink offering on it.
He poured oil on it.
God ascends.
Jacob responds.
For the first time: a drink offering.
The stone of chapter twenty eight, oil only,
becomes an altar with a drink offering and oil.
The worship deepens.
The vessel that began with a conditional vow now pours out,
not just oil, but a drink offering.
The Cup that was held is now poured.
The vessel that said if now says: here.
Take it.
All of it.
Jacob called the name of the place where God spoke with him,
Bethel.
They traveled from Bethel.
There was still some distance to come to Ephrath.
Rachel travailed.
She had hard labor.
Rachel.
The beloved wife.
The woman who drew water for ten camels.
The woman Jacob worked fourteen years for.
The woman who said give me children, or I die.
The woman God remembered.
The woman who named Joseph, may the Lord add.
She is dying now.
The Cup that was filled at a well is being emptied on a road.
When she was in hard labor, the midwife said to her:
Do not be afraid, for now you will have another son.
Another son.
Rachel asked for more.
Add.
And God added.
But the adding costs her life.
The Cup that was filled when God opened her womb is now poured out in childbirth.
The woman who said give me children or I die,
dies while having a child.
As her soul was departing, for she died, she named him Ben-oni,
Son of My Sorrow.
But his father called him Benjamin, Son of the Right Hand.
The mother names him for her pain.
The father names him for his place.
Ben-oni: the last word of a dying woman.
Benjamin:
the first word of a father who refuses to let death be the name.
The Cup of the covenant produces a son whose first name is grief and whose second name is strength.
The same pattern as the names, the mother names, the father renames.
Sarah named Isaac, laughter.
Rebekah's oracle named Jacob, heel-catcher.
Now Rachel names Benjamin, son of my sorrow.
And Jacob renames him, son of the right hand.
Rachel died and was buried on the way to Ephrath, that is,
Bethlehem.
Jacob set up a pillar on her grave.
It is the Pillar of Rachel's Grave to this day.
The beloved wife is buried on the road.
Not in a tomb.
Not at Machpelah.
On the way.
The woman who was carried out of Haran with the promise is buried between Bethel and Bethlehem.
The first wife of the covenant to die in childbirth.
The first grave on a road.
The Cup that was drawn at a well is planted on a path.
The pillar that marks her grave stands where travelers pass,
so that everyone who walks the road to Bethlehem passes the woman who said add.
Israel traveled and spread his tent beyond the tower of Eder.
Israel.
The text now calls him Israel.
The name has taken.
While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah,
his father's concubine.
And Israel heard of it.
Reuben.
The firstborn.
The son Leah named: the Lord has seen my affliction.
The boy whose name was a prayer for love.
Now he takes his father's concubine.
The same pattern as chapter thirty five's surrounding sins, seeing, taking, violating.
The firstborn, the one who should carry the Cup,
defiles the bed of the one who holds it.
Israel heard.
The father who was silent at Shechem now hears.
But the text does not say he acted.
He heard.
The silence of chapter thirty-four is not repeated,
but neither is there a response.
The hearing will carry its weight until the final blessing in chapter forty-nine:
Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might,
and the beginning of my strength, unstable as water,
you shall not excel.
Now the sons of Jacob were twelve.
Twelve.
The full count.
The Cup of the covenant now holds twelve sons, six from Leah,
two from Rachel, two from Bilhah, two from Zilpah.
The promise that was spoken to a childless couple in Ur now rests in a household of twelve men.
The dust has begun to count itself.
The stars have started to gather.
The nation is being formed, not in perfection, not in purity,
but in the mixed, stained, cleansed,
confirmed reality of a family that has carried the Cup through every kind of vessel.
Jacob came to Isaac his father, to Mamre, to Kiriath-arba, that is,
Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac lived as foreigners.
Hebron.
Machpelah.
The cave Abraham bought for Sarah.
The field where the first acre of the promise was a grave.
Jacob returns to his father.
The son who left as a deceiver returns as Israel.
The man who stole a blessing comes back to the father who trembled when he discovered the theft.
The days of Isaac were one hundred eighty years.
Isaac breathed his last and died and was gathered to his people,
old and full of days.
Esau and Jacob his sons buried him.
The brothers meet again.
At a grave.
The same way Abraham's sons met, Isaac and Ishmael at Machpelah.
Now Esau and Jacob, at Hebron.
The brothers who struggled in the womb,
who were divided by a birthright,
who were separated by a stolen blessing,
who were reconciled at the Jabbok, stand together at their father's grave.
The Cup that was carried by Isaac is now held by Israel.
The father who trembled is gathered to his people.
The brothers who wept at their reunion now bury their father in silence.
The Cup of return is complete.
The vessel has come home.
It has been cleansed of idols, confirmed in name,
filled with the promise of kings,
marked by the death of the beloved wife,
stained again by the firstborn's sin,
and brought to the grave of the father who held it before him.
The Cup is not clean.
But it is home.
And the twelve who carry it are the beginning of something that none of them can see,
a nation, a kingdom,
a people that will carry this Cup through Egypt and through wilderness and through exile and through silence and through the long road that leads to a manger in the town where Rachel is buried.
